newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel calls for faster regional privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Waigel calls for faster regional privatisation.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday appealed to regional and local authorities to step up the pace of privatisation or risk derailing long-term plans for the state to reduce its role in the economy.
Speaking to managers of state-owned firms, Waigel said that states and municipalities were lagging the federal government -- threatening to put them on a collision course with Bonn.
"Against this background I have little understanding for financial demands from local authorities to the federal government," Waigel said.
Calling for more teamwork between Bonn and the regions in Europe's largest economy, he said: "Whoever does not understand this risks forcing a crisis of federalism."

Germany will put a slice of telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom AG on the stock market in November and talks to sell Deutsche Postbank AG are under way. The postal service and a series of other enterprises are slated for privatisation.

Waigel's speech signalled the end of a summer break marked by deadlock over a tough austerity package and a swirl of tax-cutting proposals aimed at getting Germany fit for European monetary union in 1999.
Germany is struggling to cut its budget deficit to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product next year so that it can meet one of the Maastricht treaty's key criteria for joining EMU.
Waigel has resisted calls from the opposition Social Democrats and his own coalition partners, the Free Democrats, to enact a major tax reform before elections due in 1998.

Setting out his broad policy objectives, Waigel said he wanted to cut the level of state spending to 46 percent of GDP by the year 2000 -- putting expenditure in line with the level before German reunification in 1989.

Waigel said he would only let expenditures grow by one percent per year, below expected economic growth. Meanwhile, 25 billion marks in federal spending cuts are included in the 1997 budget -- which should be matched by Germany's 16 states.
"These are necessary and defensible measures needed to avoid more drastic action later," Waigel said. "I call that responsible financial policy."
Waigel's draft budget was rejected before the summer recess by the upper house of parliament, in which the states are represented, and is being reviewed by an arbitration committee.

He said it was vital to pass the budget law on time to ensure cuts in levies on investment and enterprise take effect. Waigel's draft would abolish asset tax, reform inheritance and company taxes and cut the solidarity surcharge.
"We are pursuing a policy of providing for growth in order to create jobs," Waigel said. German unemployment, at nearly four million, is near post-war highs.
